title: A High Priest Called by God, and a Call to Grow Up
summary: Every high priest is chosen from among people to represent them before God, deals gently with the ignorant because he is weak himself, and must be called by God as Aaron was. Christ did not appoint himself either: God named him Son and a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek. In his earthly life he prayed with loud cries and tears, learned obedience through suffering, and became the source of eternal salvation. The author wants to say more but stops to rebuke his readers for needing milk when they should be ready for solid food.
story: Chapter 4 ended by introducing Jesus as the great high priest. Chapter 5 now asks what qualifies anyone to be a high priest and shows that Jesus meets the qualifications, though in an unexpected way. It introduces the mysterious figure of Melchizedek, whom the author will explain in chapter 7. But before he can, he stops. His readers are not ready for the deeper teaching, and verses 11-14 begin the third warning passage, which runs through chapter 6. The chapter thus holds together two things the letter never separates: the glory of Christ's priesthood and the danger of a congregation too sluggish to take it in.
historical:
Israel's high priesthood was established in the line of Aaron, Moses' brother, whom God appointed (Exodus 28 and 29, Numbers 16 and 17). The story of Korah's rebellion in Numbers 16 shows what happened to those who took the honor on themselves. By the first century the high priesthood in Jerusalem had become entangled with politics; Herod the Great and later the Roman governors appointed and removed high priests at will, and the office was dominated by a few wealthy families. The ideal the author describes (called by God, compassionate, conscious of his own weakness) stood in contrast to that reality, though he does not mention the contemporary priests directly.

Verse 7 recalls Jesus' prayers in Gethsemane before his arrest, when he asked the Father to let the cup pass from him and yet submitted to his will (Mark 14:32-36). The Gospels do not mention loud cries and tears in Gethsemane specifically, though Luke describes his anguish and sweat like drops of blood (Luke 22:44, a verse missing from some early manuscripts), and the cries may also recall his cry from the cross.
cultural:
In the ancient world, a priest was a go-between who stood for the people before God, bringing their gifts and sacrifices, and stood for God before the people, pronouncing blessing and instruction. The high priest's most solemn duty was the Day of Atonement, when he offered sacrifice first for his own sins and then for the people's (Leviticus 16:6, 15), a detail the author mentions in verse 3.

The contrast of milk and solid food was a common teaching image in the ancient world. Greek philosophers such as Epictetus used it for the difference between beginners and advanced students, and Paul used it with the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 3:1-2). The term translated mature (teleios) was used for those who had completed their training. The author's rebuke would have stung: people who had been believers long enough to teach others still needed the basics repeated.
literary: Verses 1-10 are built as a comparison between the ordinary high priest and Christ, matching point for point. Verses 1-4 set out three features of a high priest: he is chosen from among men to act for them before God (verse 1); he can deal gently with the ignorant because he shares their weakness (verses 2-3); and he does not take the honor for himself but is called (verse 4). Verses 5-10 answer these in reverse order: Christ was called by God (verses 5-6); he shared human weakness in suffering and prayer (verses 7-8); and he became the source of salvation for others (verses 9-10). Two quotations support his call: Psalm 2:7, already used in 1:5, and Psalm 110:4, which will become the key text of chapter 7. Verses 11-14 break off abruptly with a direct address to the readers, a sharp change of tone that is typical of the sermon's rhythm of teaching and exhortation.

outline.t: Christ appointed by God as Son and priest forever
Prayers, tears, obedience, and eternal salvation
Rebuke: still on milk when you should be teachers

doctrines.note: Jesus is both Son and priest. He did not claim the office for himself but was appointed by God with words from two psalms, Psalm 2:7 and Psalm 110:4, which join royal and priestly roles in one person.
Having completed his obedience through suffering, Christ became "the source of eternal salvation" (verse 9). His priestly work is not a ritual repeated but a salvation that lasts.
Jesus' own prayer life was marked by loud cries and tears. He was heard because of his reverent submission, though the answer was not deliverance from death but through it, in resurrection.
Maturity is not information but trained discernment: the mature have exercised their senses by practice to tell good from evil (verse 14).

words.note: Melchisedek, Melchizedek, the priest-king of Salem who met Abraham in Genesis 14. The name appears first here in Hebrews through Psalm 110:4, and the author will explain its significance in chapter 7. He is a priest outside the line of Aaron and the pattern for a priesthood that does not depend on descent.

Eulabeia, reverence, godly fear, or devout submission. Jesus was heard because of his eulabeia (verse 7). The word describes the attitude of one who takes God seriously and yields to his will. The same root appears in 11:7 for Noah's godly fear and in 12:28 for acceptable worship.

Hupakoe, obedience, from a root meaning to listen under. The Son learned obedience through what he suffered (verse 8), which does not mean he was once disobedient. It means he learned by experience what obedience costs, and his obedience was tested and proven to the end.

Teleios, mature, complete, perfect. It belongs to the same family of words as made perfect in verse 9. Christ was made perfect for his office; the readers are called to become mature, trained by constant practice (verse 14).

christ: This chapter shows the humanity of Jesus with unusual directness. He prayed "with loud cries and tears" to the One who could save him from death, and "learned obedience from what He suffered". He is a high priest who knows weakness from inside, though without sin. He was also appointed by God with a double title, Son and priest forever, drawn from two psalms about the Messiah. The chapter sets up a claim that will be explained in chapter 7: that Jesus holds a priesthood not like Aaron's, based on ancestry and ended by death, but like Melchizedek's, eternal and given by God's own word. And his obedience makes him "the source of eternal salvation to all who obey Him".

hard.q: If Jesus was heard in his prayer to be saved from death, why did he die?
hard.a:
Verse 7 says Jesus prayed to the One who could save him from death and "was heard because of His reverence". Yet he was crucified. Interpreters offer several explanations. One is that his prayer was ultimately a prayer for God's will to be done, as in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36), and that request was granted. Another, favored by many commentators, is that he was saved out of death rather than from dying: God answered by raising him from the dead, as the Greek preposition can mean out of as well as from. A third view connects the prayer to his whole passion, heard in that God sustained him through it.

These readings agree on the chapter's point. Jesus' prayer was genuine anguish, not playacting, and God's answer was not escape from suffering but victory through it. The author offers this to readers who were suffering and praying and perhaps wondering whether they were heard.

questions: The ideal high priest deals gently with others because he knows his own weakness. How does awareness of your own failures affect the way you treat others?
Jesus prayed with loud cries and tears. What does that permit in your own prayers?
The author says maturity comes by constant practice in distinguishing good from evil. What habits have trained your judgment, and which ones have dulled it?
